mechanism: IRIS encodes each raw frame into a small set of discrete tokens via a VQ-VAE-style autoencoder, then feeds the full sequence of (token, action, reward, done) tuples into a causal Transformer that autoregressively predicts the next frame's tokens plus reward and termination. Because the Transformer attends over the entire imagined trajectory, it can maintain long-range context across many steps. The policy is trained purely on these imagined rollouts, so real-environment samples only need to teach the world model, not the policy directly.
invariant: Compressing observations into a compact discrete vocabulary before sequence modeling reduces the prediction space enough that a general-purpose sequence model can learn accurate multi-step dynamics from few examples — the discrete bottleneck controls compounding error regardless of the specific environment's visual complexity.
prediction: IRIS's advantage over recurrent world models (e.g., DreamerV2) should grow with imagination rollout length: longer imagined trajectories compound token-prediction errors less for the Transformer than for an RNN, so ablating the Transformer in favour of an LSTM while keeping the discrete autoencoder fixed should degrade performance more steeply as rollout depth increases.
failure_mode: If the discrete autoencoder's codebook fails to cover the observation space — e.g., in environments with high visual diversity or continuous fine-grained details — the tokenised representation loses information that the Transformer cannot recover, causing the imagined rollouts to diverge from reality and the policy to overfit to hallucinated dynamics.
source_excerpt: IRIS, a data-efficient agent that learns in a world model composed of a discrete autoencoder and an autoregressive Transformer. With the equivalent of only two hours of gameplay in the Atari 100k benchmark, IRIS achieves a mean human normalized score of 1.046, and outperforms humans on 10 out of 26 games, setting a new state of the art for methods without lookahead search.
